html:
Mesoamerican city states and chiefdoms is the map's label for the many small states of central and southern Mexico between about 800 and 1200, after the fall of Teotihuacan and before the rise of the Aztecs.

In these centuries no single power ruled the region. The land was a patchwork of towns, each with a ruler, a temple pyramid, a market and farming villages around it. People grew maize, beans and squash, traded obsidian, cacao, cotton and feathers, and played the ballgame. Towns fought, married their ruling families to each other and made alliances that shifted often.

Some grew into regional powers:

  • Tula, the Toltec capital north of the Valley of Mexico
  • Cholula, a great pilgrimage city
  • Xochicalco, a fortified hilltop city with art drawn from many regions
  • the Mixtec kingdoms of Oaxaca

In the Maya lowlands many southern cities emptied in this period, while Chichen Itza rose in the north (see Maya city states). Later peoples looked back on Toltec times as a golden age, and the rulers of the Aztec Triple Alliance claimed Toltec descent.
